description: No pressure, if you are here for the experience and want to learn while building something, this is it.
summary:
Our solution is Earth Jukebox, an album featuring four curated tracks that capture changes in our planet over time. It transforms visualisations from NASA’s Earth Information Center (EIC) into music, offering an alternative way for audiences to experience and connect with Earth through sound.

To improve accessibility for blind and low-vision users, Earth Jukebox also features a Story Mode, which plays all four tracks sequentially, with an introductory audio description before each track.

NASA’s EIC produces compelling visualisations of our changing planet, but these are primarily visual. This creates accessibility barriers for people with visual impairments, a group estimated by the World Health Organization to include at least 2.2 billion people worldwide. Even for sighted audiences, complex climate data presented through maps and charts can feel abstract, making it difficult to appreciate the significance of these changes.

Earth Jukebox transforms this data into an experience that can be heard as well as seen. Through sound, narration and captions, blind and low-vision users can follow each story without relying solely on visuals. For other audiences, music adds an immersive and emotional dimension, allowing them to hear the planet warming or a storm building as lightning spreads. As a free, browser-based website, Earth Jukebox can also be used in classrooms, museums and exhibitions, including the Earth Information Center itself.
details:
What it does and how it works

Earth Jukebox is a web app that turns four NASA Earth visualizations into music, so people can hear how the planet is changing. It is styled as a digital jukebox. On the home page, visitors pick a track from a carousel. Each track page plays its music in sync with the original NASA video or images, while a waveform reacts to the sound. Each track also has two short notes, “What you are hearing” and “Describe this visual”, and an AI narrator can read either one aloud while the music dips underneath. Play Story links all four tracks into one narrated climate story, with a spoken introduction before each track and word-by-word captions on screen.

Each track uses its own method to turn data into sound. The World After Dark divides NASA’s yearly night-lights images (2012–2023) into eight regions, each with its own voice: as a region grows brighter its note rises, and the brighter it is, the louder it plays. A Planet With a Fever reads NASA’s GISTEMP temperature record (1880–2023) for eight latitude bands. Each band plays a note that falls as the band warms. As the whole planet heats up, a heartbeat quickens, a drone fades in and the harmony drifts out of tune. The Planet Breathing reads the colours of NASA’s map of net ecosystem exchange of CO₂ (2003–2017) and converts them back to the map’s own scale. A string orchestra follows the land’s breath: a solo violin rises as northern land absorbs carbon each summer, cellos swell as it releases carbon, and the timpani rolls in 2016 and 2017, after the drought, when the land absorbed less. The Storm Gathers detects lightning flashes in NASA’s visualization of strikes seen from the International Space Station (2017–2023). Each flash plays a note placed where it struck, and in the storm section drums speed up and hit harder as more lightning appears.

Benefits

NASA’s Earth science reaches most people through images, which leaves out blind and low-vision people. Earth Jukebox makes the data audible. The music carries its shape, and the narration explains what it means. Sighted visitors gain something too: hearing a harmony fall apart makes warming felt, not just seen. The app runs in any modern browser with nothing to install, so it works both on the web and at a museum or exhibit station.

Intended impact

We want Earth science to be something everyone can experience. Our goal is a listening station for places like NASA’s Earth Information Center, where visitors who cannot see the screens can still follow the story. In the future, we plan to test the app with blind and low-vision listeners and to add more NASA datasets as new tracks.

Tools and technologies

The website is built with HTML, CSS and plain JavaScript. It uses the Web Audio API and Canvas for the live waveform and equalizer, and it is hosted on Vercel. We wrote the data-to-sound scripts in Python, using NumPy, Pillow, OpenCV, pandas, SciPy and soundfile. For the orchestral track, mido generated a MIDI score that was then performed with MuseScore 4’s Muse Sounds. The narrator voice comes from Kokoro, an open-source AI text-to-speech model, and FFmpeg was used for audio and video processing. We worked together through Git and GitHub, using personal branches, pull requests and a protected main branch. No special hardware was needed beyond our laptops.

Creativity

Instead of using one formula for every dataset, we designed each track’s sound to match what its data means. A warming band of the Earth sinks in pitch and goes out of tune. The land’s carbon cycle plays as breathing. Lightning becomes the crack and rumble of a storm. Each track also has its own style, from synthesized tones to an orchestral score to a cinematic soundscape. The four tracks still build one story, from a brightening world at night to a warming planet, struggling land and gathering storms. The jukebox design makes exploring scientific data feel like choosing a song.

Factors we considered

  • Scientific honesty: our scripts read NASA’s rendered images and videos, not the raw scientific datasets. The app says so for every track, and we used NASA’s own colour scales and timing wherever we could.
  • Synchronisation: every track is timed to its visual, so sound and image always match.
  • Accessibility: this shaped the interface. It has narration for every note, captions, music that dips under the narrator, labels for screen readers, and keyboard focus outlines.
  • Practical limits: we compressed large NASA videos to fit GitHub’s file-size limits while keeping the app easy to run anywhere.
  • Musical consistency: three of the four tracks share the key of A minor, so Play Story flows as one piece.

Use of AI

We used AI tools in two parts of the project. First, our team used AI assistant to help write and debug code for the website and the data-to-sound scripts more efficiently. Every change was reviewed and tested by the team before being merged. Second, the narrator voice is AI-generated with Kokoro, an open-source text-to-speech model, which reads our narration scripts aloud for each track and for Play Story. All of the data comes from NASA, and the team chose and checked the musical mappings.
